She tells Holmes of Roylott’s violence, Julia’s death, and her own danger; Holmes finds marks on her wrist. At Stoke Moran, she confirms the room’s suspicious features and follows Holmes’s plan by signaling and sleeping elsewhere. Roylott’s snake-poison scheme targets her, but after his death Holmes and Watson take her to her aunt at Harrow.

l: Dr. Grimesby Roylott, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes
s: Dr. Grimesby Roylott is a doctor, the last survivor of the Roylotts of Stoke Moran, and stepfather of Helen and Julia Stoner. Immensely strong, violently temperamental, and feared locally, he keeps a cheetah and baboon at Stoke Moran and has assaulted a blacksmith. Financially motivated to prevent his stepdaughters’ marriages, he is associated with Julia’s unexplained death. After Helen seeks help, Roylott confronts and threatens Holmes, bending a steel poker. He uses a swamp adder, sent through a ventilator and down a dummy bell-rope, to attack a bedroom occupant. Holmes strikes the snake, which returns to Roylott and kills him by biting him.

l: Julia Stoner (Helen Stoner's sister), The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes
s: Julia Stoner, Helen Stoner’s twin sister, was engaged to a half-pay major of marines. At Stoke Moran mansion, she occupied the middle bedroom and reported smelling Dr. Grimesby Roylott’s cigar, suggesting communication between bedrooms. After the ventilator and cord were installed, she died mysteriously two years before the account, following something linked to a low whistle; her final words referred to a “speckled band.”

l: the Roylotts of Stoke Moran, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes
s: The Roylotts of Stoke Moran are an ancient Saxon family whose once vast wealth and estate were ruined by four dissolute heirs, leaving few acres and a heavily mortgaged ancestral house.

l: Stoke Moran, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes
s: Stoke Moran is the Roylotts’ old ancestral home and estate on Surrey’s western border, containing Stoke Moran mansion. Dr. Grimesby Roylott lives there with Helen and Julia; after Julia dies there and Helen faces danger, Holmes and Watson travel to investigate.

l: Percy Armitage, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes
s: Percy Armitage, the second son of Mr. Armitage of Crane Water near Reading, is Helen Stoner's friend and intended husband. He has asked Helen to marry him, and their wedding is planned for the spring.

l: Hampshire, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes
s: Hampshire is the county where Jep hro Rucastle says he lives. The Copper Beeches is described as being five miles beyond Winchester in Hampshire.

l: the Stoke Moran manor-house, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes
s: Stoke Moran manor-house is an old ancestral, heavily mortgaged mansion of grey, lichen-blotched stone, partly ruined and divided into a central block and two wings. Only one wing, including three ground-floor bedrooms, is inhabited; Dr. Grimesby Roylott lives in its comparatively modern right-hand block. Scaffolding marks repairs as Holmes examines its exterior and internal features while investigating a death and Helen's threat.

l: the three ground-floor bedrooms, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes
s: Three ground-floor bedrooms, Dr. Roylott's, Julia's, and Helen's, open onto one corridor, have no communication between them, and their windows open onto the lawn.

l: the corridor, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes
s: The corridor connects the three ground-floor bedrooms and contains a lamp. Helen entered it after hearing Julia scream and saw Julia emerge from her room.

l: the gipsies, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes
s: The gipsies are a group allowed by Dr. Grimesby Roylott to camp on the bramble-covered land at Stoke Moran, where they are present and intimate with him. Helen first suspects they may explain a low whistle and Julia’s “speckled band,” perhaps through their spotted head handkerchiefs. Holmes treats them as possible but unproven elements of the mystery.

l: the cheetah, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes
s: is_a Indian animal [kept by Dr. Grimesby Roylott] The cheetah is one of the Indian animals kept by Dr. Grimesby Roylott and allowed to wander freely over the grounds. Its presence contributes to Helen and Julia's practice of locking their bedroom doors at night.

l: the baboon, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes
s: is_a Indian animal [kept by Dr. Grimesby Roylott] The baboon is one of the Indian animals kept by Dr. Grimesby Roylott and allowed to wander freely over the grounds. Its presence contributes to the sisters' feeling that they were not safe unless their bedroom doors were locked.

l: the low whistle, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes
s: is_heard_at three in the morning [during several nights] The low whistle was heard by Julia at about three in the morning during the nights before her death. Helen heard a similar whistle immediately after Julia screamed and again two years later when Helen slept in Julia's former room.

l: the metallic sound, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes
s: A clanging metallic sound, like falling metal, is reported by Helen shortly after the whistle during Julia Stoner’s death; Holmes questions whether the storm and old house caused confusion.

l: the speckled band, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes
s: The speckled band is Julia Stoner’s dying reference, initially uncertain and possibly thought to mean people or delirium. It is ultimately revealed as the yellow swamp adder that appears around Dr. Grimesby Roylott’s head after his death.

l: Julia Stoner's death, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes
s: Julia Stoner died in her bedroom at Stoke Moran manor-house, in the middle bedroom, two years before Helen consulted Holmes and shortly before Julia's wedding. After hearing a low whistle, she cried out, convulsed, and named a speckled band before becoming unconscious; medical aid failed. Though her locked, seemingly inaccessible room showed no poison, violence, or intruder, Holmes investigates its unusual fixtures, believing a tangible cause lay behind the unresolved mystery.

l: Helen Stoner's impending marriage, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes
s: is_to Percy Armitage [planned for the spring] Helen Stoner is engaged to Percy Armitage and expects to marry in the spring. She says her stepfather has offered no opposition, but her move into Julia's former room and the repeated whistle have caused her to fear for her safety.

l: the locked bedroom, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes
s: The sisters customarily locked their bedroom doors at night because of the cheetah and baboon. On the night of Julia's death, her door was secured from the inside, while the barred windows, solid walls, and blocked chimney appeared to exclude any intruder.

l: the five-finger bruises, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes
s: are_on Helen Stoner [on her wrist] The five-finger bruises are livid marks on Helen Stoner's wrist, showing the impressions of four fingers and a thumb. Sherlock Holmes uses them to establish that Helen has been cruelly handled, although Helen excuses Dr. Roylott by saying he may not know his own strength.

l: fear and nervous shock, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes
s: is_considered_cause_of Julia Stoner's death [Helen Stoner’s belief] Helen believes that Julia died from pure fear and nervous shock because no poison, violence, or other cause was found. Her own terror is intensified by hearing the low whistle in Julia's former room, but the text does not establish that this belief is correct.

l: the will of the deceased wife, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes
s: The deceased wife’s will provides each daughter £250 upon marriage from an estate now yielding £750 after agricultural prices fell. Holmes concludes that either daughter’s marriage would sharply reduce Roylott’s means, especially if both marry.

l: the marriage arrangement, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes
s: is_opposed_by Dr. Grimesby Roylott [because marriage would reduce his income] The marriage arrangement would give each daughter an income of £250 upon marriage. Holmes determines that the arrangement gives Dr. Grimesby Roylott a strong financial motive to prevent his stepdaughters from marrying.

l: the mystery, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes
s: concerns Helen Stoner's sister's death The mystery concerns Helen Stoner’s sister’s unexplained death, the nocturnal whistles, the dying woman’s words, and the danger now facing Helen. Holmes believes the mystery may be connected with Dr. Grimesby Roylott’s motives and the unusual construction of the bedroom.

l: the nocturnal whistles, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes
s: are_heard_at night The nocturnal whistles were heard in connection with the mysterious death at Stoke Moran. Holmes considers them alongside the gipsies, the dying woman’s words, and the other clues, but their meaning remains unresolved in this unit.

l: the dying woman’s words, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes
s: are_uttered_by Julia Stoner (Helen Stoner's sister) [at the time of her death] The dying woman’s words include an allusion to a band. Holmes treats this allusion, together with the nocturnal whistles and the presence of the gipsies, as a possible clue to the mystery.

l: the poker, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes
s: A steel fireplace tool is seized and bent into a curve by Dr. Grimesby Roylott, thrown into the fireplace, then straightened again by Sherlock Holmes.

l: the dummy bell-rope, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes
s: The dummy bell-rope hangs beside the bed in the middle bedroom, appearing to communicate with the housekeeper’s room. Holmes discovers it is not attached to a wire or bell, but is fastened by a hook above the ventilator opening. He concludes it serves as a bridge for the snake to pass from the ventilator to the bed.

l: the ventilator, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes
s: The ventilator is a small opening between the middle bedroom and Dr. Grimesby Roylott’s room, not to outside air. Installed around the time of the dummy bell-rope, it is significant to Holmes. Roylott uses it to send a snake toward the bed; Holmes attacks the snake when it emerges.

l: the shutters, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes
s: The shutters are a barred window covering, secured by metal bars and impassable when bolted; Holmes examines Helen’s room and finds their iron hinges fixed in masonry, with no opening to raise the bar.

l: the dog lash, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes
s: is_a looped whipcord [tied into a loop] A small dog lash hangs in Dr. Grimesby Roylott’s room with its end curled and tied into a loop of whipcord. Holmes considers the unusual knot significant and becomes visibly grim after examining it.

l: the iron safe, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes
s: The iron safe in Dr. Grimesby Roylott’s room contains a swamp adder and a saucer of milk; after it is removed from Roylott, Sherlock Holmes returns it and closes the safe.

l: the examination of Stoke Moran, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes
s: Sherlock Holmes conducts an examination of Stoke Moran, inspecting the mansion and bedroom features, including a bell-rope, ventilator, safe, milk saucer, chair, and dog lash; its findings strengthen suspicion of Dr. Grimesby Roylott and prompt a nighttime investigation.

l: Stoke Moran Manor House, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes
s: has the ventilator [between the relevant rooms] Stoke Moran Manor House contains the connected bedrooms, ventilator, dummy bell-rope, clamped bed, and Dr. Grimesby Roylott’s room. Sherlock Holmes and Dr. John Watson enter its grounds and investigate it during the night.

l: the swamp adder, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes
s: A snake, called India's deadliest, is identified by Sherlock Holmes as the deadly snake used by Dr. Grimesby Roylott; after biting Roylott, it is removed and locked in an iron safe.

l: the clamped bed, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes
s: The clamped bed is fastened to the floor, cannot be moved, and remains aligned with the ventilator and dummy bell-rope.

l: the snake-poison murder scheme, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes
s: The snake-poison murder scheme, devised by Dr. Grimesby Roylott, sends a trained swamp adder through a ventilator and dummy bell-rope to a bed’s clamped occupant. Roylott recalls it by whistle; its rapid, chemically undetectable poison kills the victim.

l: the death of Dr. Grimesby Roylott, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes
s: is_caused_by the swamp adder [after Holmes drives it back toward its master] The death of Dr. Grimesby Roylott occurs when the snake he used against the bedroom occupant turns upon him after Sherlock Holmes strikes at it. The official inquiry concludes that he died while indiscreetly playing with a dangerous pet.

l: Victor Hatherley, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes
s: Victor Hatherley is a young orphaned, unmarried hydraulic engineer who lives alone in London, with considerable experience from a seven-year apprenticeship to Venner & Matheson and chambers in Victoria Street. He accepts a confidential fifty-guinea night commission at Eyford from Colonel Lysander Stark. During the dangerous engagement, he is attacked and loses his thumb, receives brandy afterward, and is carried while unconscious. He identifies Dr. Becher’s burning house as the place of his confinement and escape through a window. He returns to London without the fee or thumb, though Holmes says he gained experience.

l: Colonel Lysander Stark, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes
s: Colonel Lysander Stark is a thin, apparently forty-year-old man with a German accent who owns a fuller’s-earth mining operation with associates. He hires Victor Hatherley for fifty guineas to inspect a hydraulic stamping machine at his secluded residence near Eyford, demanding secrecy and claiming it processes fuller’s-earth. When Hatherley doubts that explanation, Stark traps him in the hydraulic press, activates it, pursues him with a cleaver, and cuts off his thumb during his escape.

l: Eyford, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes
s: Eyford is a small Berkshire village or locality near Reading and the Oxfordshire border, served by a railway station. It matters as the rail-accessible centre for journeys to Colonel Lysander Stark’s remote country property and later for Inspector Bradstreet’s search. Hatherley is directed to meet Stark there, travels onward by carriage, escapes and returns to its vicinity for a morning train to Reading; afterward, the search party reaches Eyford and sees smoke from the nearby fire at Dr. Becher’s house.

l: hydraulic engineering, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes
s: Victor Hatherley works as a hydraulic engineer and has seven years of experience gained through an apprenticeship to Venner & Matheson. His professional expertise is the reason Colonel Lysander Stark seeks his opinion about a hydraulic stamping machine.

l: fuller’s-earth, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes
s: is_a valuable product [found in only one or two places in England] Fuller’s-earth is described as a valuable product found in only one or two places in England. Stark claims to have discovered a deposit on his land near Reading, linked to larger deposits on neighboring properties.
